walkthroughs.h2: Why was Brown v Board significant?
walkthroughs.body_html: NAACP Legal Defense Fund under Thurgood Marshall built precedents from 1935 (Murray v Maryland) to Sweatt v Painter (1950). Chief Justice Earl Warren's 17 May 1954 unanimous opinion held 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal'. Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation 'with all deliberate speed', allowing southern resistance to develop. Massive Resistance manifestos and White Citizens' Councils proliferated.

After Parks's arrest, the Women's Political Council distributed 35,000 leaflets calling for a boycott on 5 December 1955. The Montgomery Improvement Association elected MLK at 26 to lead. The boycott lasted 381 days. Browder v Gayle, decided 13 November 1956 and implementing 20 December, struck down bus segregation. Mass mobilisation and non-violent direct action emerged as central strategies.

Governor Orval Faubus deployed the Arkansas National Guard to block the Little Rock Nine entering Central High on 4 September 1957. President Eisenhower federalised the Guard and sent 1,000 paratroopers of the 101st Airborne, who escorted students on 25 September. The crisis demonstrated federal supremacy over state defiance and the role of media images in shifting public opinion.
